name: AGI Infrastructure
thesis: The AGI race is decided by physical capacity - compute clusters, power contracts, transformers, and data centre shells - not by model announcements.
thesisLong: Frontier AI labs are converging on the same constraint set: gigawatt-scale power, multi-year GPU supply agreements, and data centre shells that take longer to permit than the chips inside them take to depreciate. Training compute for frontier models has grown roughly 4-5x per year, which means the binding inputs are now electricity, transformers, switchgear, cooling, and land near transmission - not algorithmic ideas. Hyperscaler capex guidance for 2025-2026 sits in the hundreds of billions of dollars per year, and a rising share of it is electrical and mechanical plant rather than silicon. That makes the investable surface much wider than GPU designers: utilities signing data centre power agreements, transformer and switchgear makers, cooling specialists, electrical contractors, and land-plus-power platforms all sit on the critical path. The research question for each company is whether it owns capacity on a bottleneck that hyperscalers must clear to keep scaling. Names with contracted backlog tied to data centre buildouts carry evidence; names with AI in the deck but no backlog carry narrative.
whyNow: Hyperscaler capex guidance keeps being revised upward and multi-gigawatt campuses are being announced faster than grids can interconnect them. The bottleneck has visibly shifted from chips to power and electrical equipment, with transformer lead times stretched to multiple years.
falsifier: A sustained cut in hyperscaler capex guidance, or model efficiency gains that flatten compute demand growth, would break the buildout thesis at its base.
risks: Capex cycle turns if AI revenue disappoints
Model efficiency gains reduce compute intensity per dollar of revenue
Power constraints cap deployment and strand planned campuses
Oversupply and depreciation risk if buildout outruns demand
Valuations in obvious names already price multi-year flawless execution

name: Space Economy
thesis: Falling launch costs are turning orbit into industrial real estate, with constellations, defence space budgets, and in-space services compounding on cheaper access.
thesisLong: Reusable rockets collapsed the cost of reaching orbit by roughly an order of magnitude over a decade, and Starship-class heavy lift threatens another step change if it reaches operational cadence. Cheap mass to orbit unlocks the layers above launch: broadband and direct-to-cell constellations, Earth observation, in-space manufacturing experiments, and rapidly growing military space budgets across the US and allies. The economics concentrate at chokepoints - launch slots, spectrum rights, radiation-tolerant components, and ground infrastructure - rather than spreading evenly across the sector. Most of the value created so far sits in private companies, led by SpaceX, which makes the public-market expression narrow and pushes investor demand into a handful of listed names. That scarcity cuts both ways: the few credible public operators attract intense capital flows, while weaker names ride the narrative with little revenue. The research discipline is separating companies with contracted launches, government missions, or operating constellations from companies selling renders.
whyNow: Defence space spending is rising across US and allied budgets while commercial constellation deployment accelerates. Launch cadence records keep falling and direct-to-cell service moved from concept to early commercial operation, pulling forward demand across the whole supply chain.
falsifier: If Starship-class reuse fails to materially cut cost per kilogram, or constellation operators cannot convert subscribers at sustainable unit economics, the addressable market stays niche and most small caps never grow into their valuations.
risks: SpaceX vertical integration squeezes suppliers and competitors
Constellation economics remain unproven outside Starlink
Launch failures reset timelines and sentiment quickly
Government budgets shift with political cycles
Pre-revenue names depend on repeated dilutive raises

name: Power Grid
thesis: Electrification, data centres, and aging infrastructure are forcing the largest grid investment cycle in decades, and the equipment supply chain cannot keep up.
thesisLong: US electricity demand is growing again after two flat decades, driven by data centres, onshoring of manufacturing, and electrification of transport and heating. The grid that must absorb this growth is old: large transformers average decades in service, and replacement lead times have stretched from months to years. Transmission and distribution capex by utilities is on a multi-year upward path, and makers of transformers, switchgear, cables, and grid software report record backlogs. Interconnection queues hold years of generation and storage projects waiting for studies and upgrades, which makes grid capacity itself the scarce asset. The investable chain runs from utilities with constructive regulators, through electrical equipment manufacturers, to specialist EPC and grid-services firms. Backlog growth and pricing power are the evidence to track.
whyNow: Data centre load growth turned electricity demand forecasts upward for the first time in a generation, and utilities are filing record capital plans in response. Transformer and switchgear backlogs show the supply side is years behind demand.
falsifier: If data centre demand forecasts collapse or efficiency gains absorb load growth, utility capex plans would be trimmed and equipment backlogs would normalise, deflating the cycle.
risks: Regulated returns cap upside for utilities
Supply catches up and pricing normalises later in the cycle
Permitting reform stalls and projects slip
Interest rates raise the cost of capital-intensive buildouts

name: Nuclear & Uranium
thesis: Data centre power demand and energy security are driving a nuclear restart cycle while uranium supply remains structurally tight after a decade of underinvestment.
thesisLong: Nuclear has flipped from politically stranded to strategically favoured: governments have pledged large capacity expansions by 2050, restarts of shuttered plants are underway, and hyperscalers have signed power agreements tied to nuclear capacity. On the fuel side, a decade of low prices closed mines and starved exploration, so primary uranium production still runs below reactor requirements with the gap filled by shrinking secondary supplies. Western enrichment and conversion capacity is also constrained after sanctions pressure on Russian supply, adding a second chokepoint above mining. Small modular reactors attract serious capital and policy support but remain mostly pre-revenue, putting them in a different evidence class from operating miners and fuel-cycle companies. The research frame is to separate cash-flowing producers and fuel-cycle assets from developer narratives, and to track contracted offtake rather than spot price excitement.
bottlenecks: Enrichment and conversion capacity outside Russia
whyNow: Hyperscaler power deals, plant restarts, and bipartisan licensing reform have converged in a single cycle. Utilities are signing long-term uranium contracts again, and term prices have held strength even when spot cooled.
falsifier: A major reactor accident, SMR programs failing to convert into firm orders, or a faster-than-expected supply response from new mines would undercut both the demand and scarcity legs of the thesis.
risks: Uranium spot price volatility whipsaws sentiment
SMR timelines slip beyond the decade
Mine restarts and new supply arrive faster than expected
Public opinion can reverse on a single incident
Many small caps are explorers with no production path

name: Semiconductors
thesis: Semiconductors are the substrate of every other theme, but the AI trade has made the obvious names crowded, pushing the research edge to packaging, equipment, and analog niches.
thesisLong: AI accelerators turned leading-edge logic, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced packaging into the most scrutinised supply chain in markets. Capacity at the leading edge remains concentrated in one foundry, HBM in three memory makers, and EUV lithography in a single supplier, so the chokepoints are real even if widely known. CHIPS Act-style industrial policy in the US, Europe, and Japan is reshaping where fabs get built, subsidising a capex wave that flows to equipment and materials suppliers regardless of which chip designer wins. The crowding problem is concentration: a handful of mega caps carry most index exposure and valuations embed continued AI demand growth. The less-crowded research surface sits in advanced packaging, test, photonics, power semiconductors, and specialised materials, where AI demand pull is real but coverage is thinner. Cyclicality has not been repealed - memory and analog still swing - so position in the cycle matters as much as the secular story.
whyNow: AI accelerator demand still outruns supply at the leading edge, and packaging plus HBM remain the gating constraints on shipped compute. Subsidised fab construction across three continents is mid-build, keeping equipment order books elevated.
falsifier: An AI capex pause that leaves accelerator inventory building at customers, or a normalisation of HBM and packaging supply ahead of demand, would expose how much cyclical risk the crowded names carry.
risks: Taiwan concentration is a single geopolitical point of failure
Export controls reshape demand maps abruptly
Inventory cycles still produce sharp drawdowns
Crowded positioning amplifies any guidance miss
Custom silicon by hyperscalers shifts value capture

name: Critical Minerals
thesis: The West is rebuilding non-Chinese supply chains for rare earths, lithium, and strategic metals, with governments now acting as anchor customers and price-floor setters.
thesisLong: China controls the majority of refining and separation for rare earths, gallium, graphite, and several battery inputs, and has shown willingness to use export controls as leverage. That converted critical minerals from a commodity story into a security story: Western governments now fund mines, refiners, and magnet plants directly through defence procurement, price floors, and equity stakes. The hard part is midstream - separation, refining, and magnet making - where decades of cost advantage built Chinese dominance, so new Western capacity needs sustained subsidy to clear hurdle rates. Project timelines are long and permitting remains the binding constraint in most jurisdictions, which keeps supply inelastic when demand or policy shocks arrive. For research purposes the field splits into producers with offtake and government backing, developers with credible permits, and explorers whose value is mostly narrative. Government contract announcements are the highest-signal evidence in this theme.
bottlenecks: Rare earth separation and refining outside China
whyNow: Export-control episodes proved these supply chains can be weaponised, and Western governments responded with direct funding, offtake deals, and price supports for domestic producers. Defence and EV demand give the buildout a decade of policy tailwind.
falsifier: A durable trade detente that restores cheap Chinese supply, or sustained low prices that no subsidy regime offsets, would stall the Western buildout and strand developers.
risks: Commodity price moves swamp company execution
Permitting delays push first production out by years
Subsidy dependence creates political risk
Chinese supply responses can crash prices deliberately
Most explorers never reach production

name: Defence & Drones
thesis: Attritable autonomous systems are rewriting defence procurement, shifting budget share from exquisite platforms toward software-defined mass produced at commercial speed.
thesisLong: Ukraine demonstrated that cheap drones can destroy assets costing a thousand times more, and every Western defence ministry has absorbed the lesson. Procurement is shifting toward attritable autonomy, counter-drone systems, and replenishable munitions, with NATO members raising spending targets and new entrants winning programs that primes once owned by default. The constraint set is industrial: solid rocket motors, small turbines, non-Chinese component supply chains, and production lines that can scale to wartime rates. Software-defined defence companies argue their margin structures can look more like technology than traditional aerospace, which is the core of the re-rating debate. Evidence quality varies widely - program-of-record wins and production contracts are high signal, while letters of intent and demo videos are not.
whyNow: European rearmament budgets and US procurement reform are moving in the same direction at once, a rare alignment. Counter-drone and attritable-mass programs are being funded on accelerated timelines after battlefield lessons.
falsifier: A broad de-escalation that lets defence budgets revert toward pre-2022 baselines, or new entrants repeatedly losing programs to incumbent primes, would cap the re-rating story.
risks: Defence budgets are political and can be cut
Program wins are lumpy and timing is unpredictable
Valuations in popular names assume technology-like margins
Export restrictions limit addressable markets
Incumbent primes can co-opt the attritable category

name: Robotics & Automation
thesis: Foundation models are colliding with cheap actuators to make general-purpose robotics plausible, but the proven economics today are in industrial and warehouse automation.
thesisLong: The same transformer architectures driving language models are being applied to robot control, and capital is flowing into humanoid programs at unprecedented scale. The near-term reality is narrower: industrial arms, warehouse automation, and surgical robotics already generate revenue and are compounding with labour scarcity in manufacturing economies. Humanoids remain mostly pre-commercial, with bill-of-materials cost, battery life, reliability, and manipulation training data as the binding constraints. The supply chain - precision actuators, harmonic drives, sensors, and batteries - may capture value earlier than the platform makers, mirroring how component suppliers monetised early smartphone cycles. Research attention belongs on shipped units, installed-base growth, and component design wins rather than demo footage.
whyNow: Humanoid prototypes have moved from labs into pilot deployments at major manufacturers, and robotics foundation models are showing transfer across tasks. Labour shortages in manufacturing and logistics keep the demand case live regardless of the humanoid timeline.
falsifier: If pilot deployments fail to convert into volume orders and robots remain confined to caged industrial tasks, the general-purpose thesis collapses back to a mature automation market growing at single digits.
risks: Humanoid timelines slip by years
Most pure-play exposure is private or pre-revenue
Chinese competition compresses hardware margins
Demo-driven hype cycles inflate weak names

name: Cybersecurity
thesis: AI raises both attack volume and defence budgets, but the public-market trade is mature - value is consolidating into platforms while point solutions get squeezed.
thesisLong: Security spending is among the least discretionary lines in enterprise IT, sustained by ransomware economics, state-sponsored activity, and regulatory disclosure mandates. AI is intensifying the arms race: generated phishing, deepfake fraud, and automated vulnerability discovery raise attack volume while vendors embed AI agents into detection and response. The market structure is consolidating, with large platforms absorbing point-solution categories and buyers preferring fewer vendors, which compresses the small-cap opportunity set relative to other themes. Identity, cloud security, and security for AI systems themselves are the fastest-growing subsegments. Durable revenue and high switching costs make this a quality compounder field rather than an early-discovery one, and valuations generally reflect that.
bottlenecks: Enterprise budget fatigue and tool sprawl
whyNow: AI-generated attacks have moved from proof of concept to commodity tooling, and boards now treat breach risk as a disclosure and liability issue rather than an IT line item. Platform vendors are using AI features to force consolidation decisions.
falsifier: If AI-driven defence automates away the talent shortage faster than it scales attacks, growth in security budgets could decelerate and the sector would trade like mature software.
risks: Valuation premiums leave little room for execution slips
Consolidation kills point-solution small caps
A breach at a vendor destroys trust overnight
Budget growth decelerates with enterprise IT cycles

name: Quantum Computing
thesis: Quantum computing is a genuine long-horizon technology where error-correction milestones are real, but commercial revenue remains tiny and the listed pure plays trade far ahead of evidence.
thesisLong: Error-corrected logical qubits have moved from theory to demonstration, and credible roadmaps from major labs target useful fault-tolerant machines in the 2030s. The science is advancing on multiple hardware paths - superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, and neutral atom - with no settled winner, which makes platform risk extreme for single-name exposure. Commercial revenue across the listed pure plays remains tens of millions of dollars against multi-billion valuations, funded by repeated equity raises, so dilution is a structural feature of the field. The nearer-term monetisable layers are quantum networking, sensing, and post-quantum cryptography migration, which piggybacks on classical security budgets. Government funding is substantial and rising across the US, Europe, and China, providing a revenue floor for some names. The honest research frame is venture-style: small position context, milestone tracking, and an expectation that most current names will not be the eventual winners.
bottlenecks: Qubit error rates and correction overhead
Absence of commercial workloads at scale
whyNow: Error-correction demonstrations and rising government programs have pulled the credible timeline forward, and retail flows have made the listed pure plays among the most traded speculative names. The gap between scientific progress and revenue is the defining feature of the moment.
falsifier: If logical-qubit scaling stalls for several years or classical algorithms keep matching claimed quantum advantages, the commercial timeline pushes past 2040 and the funding model for pure plays breaks.
risks: Revenue is negligible relative to valuations
Continuous dilution funds operations
Hardware platform risk - the winning modality is unknown
Retail-driven volatility produces violent drawdowns
Big tech in-house programs may capture the value

name: Fusion Energy
thesis: Hyperscaler PPAs (Google-CFS 200MW, Microsoft-Helion) and a record $4.48B private funding year have pulled fusion's commercial clock forward, but zero fusion electrons have ever been delivered to a grid and nearly all pure-plays are private - public-market exposure is thin, indirect, and supplier-shaped.
thesisLong: Fusion crossed a threshold between 2023 and 2026: it stopped being purely a science program and became a contracted commercial bet. Microsoft signed the world's first fusion power purchase agreement with Helion in May 2023 for at least 50MW with initial operations targeted for 2028, and Helion broke ground on its Orion plant in Malaga, Washington in July 2025, receiving a Chelan County conditional use permit in October 2025. Google followed on June 30, 2025 with a 200MW PPA from Commonwealth Fusion Systems' first ARC plant in Chesterfield County, Virginia, targeted for the early 2030s and explicitly anchored to CFS' SPARC tokamak demonstrating net fusion energy (Q greater than 1); SPARC construction passed roughly 75% complete in April 2026, with first plasma now targeted for 2027 - a slip from the 2026 operations date stated at the PPA announcement - and the net energy attempt to follow (the first HTS toroidal-field magnet, TF1, was installed in the Devens tokamak hall in early 2026, per CFS and press reports). Capital has responded: the Fusion Industry Association's 2026 report recorded $4.48B raised in the 12 months to mid-2026, up 69% year on year, taking cumulative sector funding to roughly $14.2B since 2021, led by CFS ($863M), Proxima Fusion ($518M), Helion ($465M) and Inertia Enterprises ($450M). Policy is also constructive: the US DOE Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program committed $46M across 8 companies (agreements signed June 2024), opened to new entrants in June 2025, and DOE created a dedicated Office of Fusion in its November 20, 2025 reorganization. The honest gap is the core of this vertical: no fusion machine anywhere has delivered net electricity, the PPAs are milestone-conditioned commitments rather than delivered energy, and the public-sector benchmark ITER now targets deuterium-tritium operations in 2039 under its 2024 rebaseline - a reminder that fusion timelines slip by years, not months. Nearly every credible fusion developer (CFS, Helion, TAE, Tokamak Energy, Pacific Fusion, Proxima) is private, so listed exposure is limited to diversified giants (offtakers like Alphabet and Microsoft, energy majors with venture stakes) and adjacent suppliers of magnets, materials, and power systems whose fusion revenue is a small slice of their business. Lyra tracks this vertical research-first: the tradeable surface today is narrow and mostly indirect, and the key watch item is whether SPARC's Q greater than 1 attempt and Helion's 2028 delivery date convert contracts into electrons.
bottlenecks: Net-electricity demonstration - Q greater than 1 engineering gain has never been achieved by any private machine; SPARC's post-first-plasma attempt (first plasma targeted 2027, slipped from 2026) is the gating milestone
High-temperature superconducting (REBCO) magnet and tape supply for tokamak builds
Tritium fuel-cycle closure and breeding-blanket technology - no commercial-scale tritium breeding exists
Plasma-facing materials that survive continuous high heat and neutron flux
Public-market access - nearly all pure-plays are private, so listed exposure is indirect supplier exposure
Licensing and regulatory capacity as first-of-a-kind plants (Orion, ARC) move through permitting
whyNow: SPARC construction passed roughly 75% complete in April 2026, with first plasma targeted for 2027 (slipped from 2026) and a net-fusion-energy attempt to follow; Helion's Orion plant broke ground July 2025 against a 2028 Microsoft delivery date and cleared its Chelan County conditional use permit in October 2025; the FIA's 2026 report logged a record $4.48B funding year driven partly by AI data-center demand; and DOE created a dedicated Office of Fusion in its November 20, 2025 reorganization after reopening its Milestone program to new teams in June 2025 - the next 24 months contain the sector's most consequential go/no-go milestones ever scheduled.
falsifier: If SPARC fails to demonstrate net fusion energy (Q greater than 1) by end-2028, or Helion misses 2028 first-power and the Microsoft PPA is quietly renegotiated or lapses, the near-term commercialization thesis collapses back to an ITER-style 2040s horizon and the vertical should be demoted to watch-only.
risks: Technology risk: no fusion device has ever delivered net electricity to a grid - every PPA is conditional on milestones not yet met
Timeline risk: ITER's 2024 rebaseline pushed deuterium-tritium operations to 2039, a 4-year slip - private roadmaps inherit the same slip tendency

Access risk: pure-plays are private, so listed 'fusion exposure' is mostly suppliers and offtakers whose fusion revenue share is small - narrative-driven repricing of quasi-exposed small caps can reverse fast
Concentration risk: over half of the record 2025-26 funding went to just four private companies
Fuel risk: deuterium-tritium designs depend on scarce tritium and unproven breeding; alternative fuels (D-He3) carry their own physics risk
Crowding risk: AI-datacenter energy narrative is pulling generalist capital into a sector with almost no revenue
